content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published a protocol for the surveillance of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) attributable to viral hepatitis in clinical centers of excellence. This document outlines the terms of use, emphasizing that the work can be copied, redistributed, and adapted for non-commercial purposes, provided it is appropriately cited. However, the use of the WHO logo is prohibited, and any adaptations must be licensed under the same or an equivalent Creative Commons license. If the work is translated, a disclaimer must be included, stating that WHO is not responsible for the content or accuracy of the translation, and the original English version remains the authoritative edition. The protocol highlights the importance of mortality data in viral hepatitis surveillance, focusing on acute hepatitis (new infections), chronic hepatitis B (HBV) and C (HCV) prevalence, and mortality from sequelae such as cirrhosis and HCC. Reducing mortality from HBV and HCV is a key criterion for achieving the elimination of hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030, as outlined in the Global Health Sector Strategy (GHSS). Countries are encouraged to develop systematic methods to estimate mortality from HBV and HCV infections, which have historically been underreported due to limitations in International Classification of Disease (ICD) coding. Since 2010, the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) project has provided estimates of global mortality from chronic HBV and HCV infections, accounting for deaths from cirrhosis and HCC based on their viral causes. This approach involves estimating the proportion of cirrhosis and HCC cases attributable to HBV and HCV at national, regional, and global levels using published studies. WHO and GBD now use this method to estimate mortality. At the national level, most countries lack systematic processes to generate mortality estimates for viral hepatitis. The protocol recommends institutionalizing methods used in previous studies and integrating them into routine surveillance systems. To estimate national hepatitis-related mortality, countries need to (1) estimate mortality from chronic liver disease (including cirrhosis and HCC) and (2) determine the fraction of these conditions attributable to hepatitis viruses. National mortality data are often available, but in countries with suboptimal data quality, estimates from WHO or GBD can be used. The protocol also emphasizes the need to estimate the prevalence of HBV/HDV co-infection in patients with cirrhosis and HCC in countries where hepatitis D virus (HDV) is a public health concern. This information can be used to calculate the fractions of cirrhosis and HCC attributable to HBV, HCV, and HDV, which in turn can inform national mortality rates. Advances in antiviral treatments for HBV and HCV necessitate updated estimates of these fractions for all patients with cirrhosis or HCC, those with late-stage liver disease, and those undergoing liver transplantation. The objectives of the protocol include recruiting a suitable sample of patients with cirrhosis and HCC, assessing their HBV, HCV, and HDV status through medical record reviews, estimating the proportion of patients with these infections, and providing input for national mortality estimates. Surveillance activities will focus on patients hospitalized or seen as outpatients in referral hepatology or gastroenterology centers. Investigators will extract data from medical records using a standardized case report form, including information on age, sex, alcohol intake, metabolic syndrome components, and viral hepatitis infections. The protocol outlines two design options: prospective data collection, which is ideal, and retrospective data collection, which may be used initially to generate preliminary estimates. Reference centers will be selected to reflect geographical and sociological diversity, and liver transplantation centers will also be included. Sampling will involve consecutive recruitment of patients meeting case definitions until the required sample size is reached. The estimated sample size is approximately 250 cases of cirrhosis and HCC per center. Data collection will include demographic and clinical information, as well as risk factors for cirrhosis and HCC. No additional data or blood tests will be required beyond routine clinical care. Patients will be informed about the surveillance activity and given the option to opt out. The analysis plan includes estimating the attributable fraction of cirrhosis and HCC cases due to HBV, HCV, and HDV infections and applying these fractions to national mortality estimates. Data will be managed securely, and only aggregated results will be shared. The protocol has been reviewed and approved by an independent scientific review team and may require ethics committee clearance depending on national regulations. Expected outputs include a suitable sample of patients with cirrhosis and HCC, estimates of the proportion of these patients infected with HBV, HCV, or both, and improved national mortality estimates. The project aims to build capacity for HBV and HCV surveillance, generate lessons for future extensions, and foster partnerships with clinicians and laboratory specialists. Cost considerations include training workshops, data collection support, biomarker testing kits, and dissemination activities. In the future, the pilot projects are expected to generate high-quality, sustainable information, with clinical centers of excellence serving as resource partners for testing and treatment activities.
